results.response: Yes—Jeju Island is worth including if you enjoy volcanic landscapes, coastal scenery, waterfalls, hiking, beaches, and distinctive local food. Highlights include Hallasan National Park, Seongsan Ilchulbong, Manjanggul Cave, and the Olle walking trails; allow at least 2–4 days, as the island is larger and more spread out than it appears. Jeju is especially pleasant in spring and autumn, while summer is popular for beaches but can be humid and rainy; a rental car is convenient, though buses and taxis cover major areas. Plan routes and check attractions through the official Jeju tourism site: https://www.visitjeju.net/en/

results.question: I heard Jeju black pork has too much fat and is a tourist trap. Is this true?
results.response: Jeju black pork is naturally well-marbled, so it often has a thicker, richer fat layer than ordinary pork—but that is part of its appeal, not necessarily a sign of poor quality. It is not inherently a tourist trap, although restaurants in major visitor areas may charge premium prices or serve ordinary pork under vague “black pork” branding. Look for restaurants stating **Jeju native black pig (제주흑돼지)**, clear origin labeling, high local reviews, and a busy local clientele; ask whether the meat is 제주산 and 흑돼지 before ordering. The official Jeju tourism site has food and restaurant information: https://www.visitjeju.net/ (English available).

results.question: Does Jeju Island charge an entry tax or environmental fee for tourists arriving at the airport?
results.response: No. **Jeju Island does not currently charge tourists an entry tax or environmental fee when they arrive at Jeju International Airport**, whether arriving from mainland Korea or abroad. Airport and passenger-service charges—plus any applicable departure-related tourism levy—are generally included in the airline ticket, not collected as an arrival fee. For current travel notices, check the official [Jeju Tourism Organization](https://www.visitjeju.net/en) and [Korea Airports Corporation–Jeju Airport](https://www.airport.co.kr/jejueng/main.do) websites.

results.question: Is Jeju Island suffering from overtourism? Should I avoid visiting?
results.response: Jeju does experience overtourism pressures in specific places—especially Seongsan Ilchulbong, Hallasan, popular beaches, and some coastal cafés—during summer, holidays, and peak foliage seasons, rather than uniformly across the whole island. You do not need to avoid Jeju; visiting in spring or late autumn, traveling on weekdays, and exploring less-visited areas can reduce congestion and support local communities. Reserve Hallasan trails where required, follow parking and environmental rules, and consider buses or smaller local businesses instead of concentrating your trip around major attractions. Check current trail, weather, and visitor information through the official [Jeju Tourism Organization](https://www.visitjeju.net/en) and [Hallasan National Park](https://www.jeju.go.kr/hallasan/index.htm).

results.question: Is it true that foreign tourists are banned from renting cars in Jeju due to environmental concerns?
results.response: No. Foreign tourists are generally allowed to rent cars in Jeju, provided they present a passport, a valid driver’s license, and usually an International Driving Permit (IDP) recognized in South Korea; rental companies may also impose age, driving-experience, and credit-card requirements. Jeju has introduced and discussed measures to manage traffic and environmental impacts, but these are not a blanket ban on foreign renters. Check the specific company’s requirements before booking and consult [Visit Jeju](https://www.visitjeju.net/en) or [Korea Tourism Organization](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/).

results.question: What is Jeju's Carbon Free Island 2030 initiative? How is the island pursuing clean energy?
results.response: Jeju’s **Carbon Free Island 2030 (CFI 2030)** is a provincial initiative launched in 2012 to make the island’s electricity system carbon-free and transition its transportation sector away from fossil fuels by 2030. It pursues this through large-scale **onshore and offshore wind power, solar generation, energy-storage systems, smart grids, demand management, and modernization of the electricity network** to accommodate variable renewable energy. Jeju is also promoting **electric vehicles and charging infrastructure**, while exploring green hydrogen and other clean-energy technologies; however, the 2030 goals remain challenging because renewable-energy intermittency and grid constraints have caused curtailment. Official information is available from Jeju Province’s [Carbon Free Island 2030 site](https://www.jeju.go.kr/cfi/index.htm).

results.question: What incentives does Jeju offer for foreign companies or startups to set up operations on the island?
results.response:
Jeju offers eligible foreign-invested projects support through **Jeju Investment Promotion Zones** and JDC development areas, including possible land/lease assistance, infrastructure support, administrative “one-stop” services, and reductions or exemptions on certain local taxes; benefits depend on industry, investment size, employment, and location.  
Companies may also qualify for Korea-wide incentives under the **Foreign Investment Promotion Act**, such as cash grants for high-tech, R&D, or employment-generating projects, plus tax and customs benefits in designated zones—see [Invest Korea](https://www.investkorea.org).  
For startups, the **Jeju Creative Economy Innovation Center**, Jeju Business Agency, and Jeju Techno Park provide incubation, mentoring, commercialization grants, coworking, and investor connections, although many programs require a Korean entity or local registration; see the [Jeju CCEI](https://ccei.creativekorea.or.kr/jeju/) and [Jeju Business Agency](https://www.jba.or.kr/).  
The best starting point for a tailored eligibility check is [JDC’s English investment portal](https://www.jdcenter.com/eng/) or Jeju Province’s investment office, since incentives and application windows change frequently.

results.question: Is Jeju Island a good destination for digital nomads? Are there coworking spaces and fast internet?
results.response: Yes—Jeju is a good destination for digital nomads who value nature, a relaxed lifestyle, cafés, and easy access to hiking and beaches, though it can feel slower and less internationally connected than Seoul. Fast fiber internet and 5G are widely available in hotels, apartments, cafés, and coworking facilities; coworking and workation hubs are concentrated around Jeju City and Seogwipo, with current options listed on the official [Jeju Workation website](https://workation.jeju.go.kr/) and [Jeju Center for Creative Economy & Innovation](https://ccei.creativekorea.or.kr/jeju/). Public transport is adequate in cities but a rental car is often useful, and Korean-language support may be limited outside major tourist areas. For longer stays, check South Korea’s Digital Nomad/Workation visa requirements through [HiKorea](https://www.hikorea.go.kr/) and general destination information at [Visit Jeju](https://www.visitjeju.net/).

results.question: What international schools are available in Jeju Island for expat families?
results.response:
Jeju’s main international schools are concentrated in **Jeju English Education City** in Seogwipo:

- **North London Collegiate School Jeju (NLCS Jeju)** — British curriculum, including IGCSE and IB Diploma: https://www.nlcsjeju.co.kr  
- **Branksome Hall Asia** — Canadian/Ontario-based curriculum and IB programs; girls’ day school with coeducational boarding: https://www.branksome.asia  
- **Korea International School Jeju (KIS Jeju)** — American-style curriculum with AP courses: https://www.kis.ac/jeju  
- **St. Johnsbury Academy Jeju (SJA Jeju)** — American curriculum with AP courses: https://www.sjeju.org  

Admissions, age ranges, boarding availability, tuition, and Korean residency requirements vary, so families should confirm directly with each school; Jeju’s official English Education City information is available through the Jeju Free International City Development Center (JDC): https://www.jdcenter.com.

results.question: What role does Jeju play in South Korea's green hydrogen economy?
results.response: Jeju is South Korea’s leading **test bed for green hydrogen**, using its abundant wind and solar power to produce hydrogen through water electrolysis and absorb surplus renewable electricity. The island is developing an integrated hydrogen ecosystem—including production, storage, distribution, fuel-cell power generation, and hydrogen buses—to support its goal of becoming carbon-free under the **Carbon-Free Island Jeju by 2030** initiative. Its projects are intended to demonstrate how hydrogen can stabilize an isolated power grid and decarbonize transport and industry, although Jeju remains primarily a demonstration and scale-up site rather than a major commercial producer. Official information is available from [Jeju Special Self-Governing Province](https://www.jeju.go.kr/) and Korea’s [Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy](https://www.motie.go.kr/).

results.question: Is there a private space industry hub in Jeju? What companies are involved?
results.response: (no response)

results.question: What is the official Jeju tourism website for planning a trip?
results.response:
The official Jeju tourism website is **Visit Jeju**: https://www.visitjeju.net/en  
It provides information on attractions, accommodations, food, festivals, transportation, travel courses, and maps.

results.question: What happens if my flight to/from Jeju is cancelled due to typhoon or heavy snow? What support is available?
results.response: If a flight to or from Jeju is cancelled because of a typhoon, heavy snow, strong winds, or other safety-related weather, the airline will generally offer **free rebooking on the next available flight or a full refund without cancellation fees**; policies and limits vary, especially for connecting or separately booked tickets. Airlines are usually **not required to provide cash compensation, hotels, meals, or ground transportation** when the cause is severe weather, although some may offer assistance—check directly with your airline or booking agency. Monitor your flight and airport notices, keep receipts, and contact your travel-insurance provider about covered additional expenses; do not go to the airport unless your airline confirms the flight is operating. Official updates are available from **Jeju International Airport/Korea Airports Corporation** ([airport.co.kr/jeju](https://www.airport.co.kr/jeju/cms/frCon/index.do?MENU_ID=220)) and the **Korea Meteorological Administration** ([weather.go.kr](https://www.weather.go.kr/eng/)).

results.question: Do I need a visa to visit Jeju Island? Is there a visa-free entry policy?
results.response: Visa requirements for Jeju Island depend on your **passport nationality, travel purpose, and route**. Jeju has a **visa-free entry program—generally up to 30 days—for citizens of many countries**, often requiring direct arrival in Jeju and limiting travel to the island; travelers who plan to visit mainland Korea should verify whether a Korean visa or separate permission is required. Visa-exempt visitors may also need **K-ETA**, unless their nationality or an active temporary exemption applies, so check before departure. Confirm your exact eligibility through the [Korea Visa Portal](https://www.visa.go.kr/), [K-ETA official site](https://www.k-eta.go.kr/), or [Korea Immigration Service](https://www.immigration.go.kr/).

results.question: Are there English-speaking hospitals or clinics in Jeju for foreign tourists in an emergency?
results.response: Yes. In an emergency, call **119** for an ambulance and say **“English, please”**; interpretation can usually be arranged, though English-speaking staff may not be available at every facility or every hour. Major Jeju hospitals with international/English-support services include **Jeju National University Hospital** ([jejunu.ac.kr/medical](https://www.jejunuh.co.kr/)) and **Halla Hospital** ([hallahospital.co.kr](https://www.hallahospital.co.kr/)); call ahead when possible to confirm language support. For the nearest open emergency department, use Korea’s official **E-Gen emergency medical portal**: [e-gen.or.kr/egen/eng_main.do](https://www.e-gen.or.kr/egen/eng_main.do). The Korea Tourism Organization’s **1330** helpline ([visitkorea.or.kr](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/)) can also provide multilingual travel and medical-navigation assistance, but call **119 first** for urgent symptoms.
